title: Pauri 8, meaning: the power of listening
hook: by listening one becomes a sage, knows earth and sky, and death cannot touch the devotee (Japji 8)
tomorrow: Pauri 9: listening, the gods and scriptures

segments.voice: Yesterday, the soft word suniai, by listening, that opens four pauris of Japji. Your line was suniai, listening.

The best listeners aren't always the ones with the best advice. They're the ones who actually stop when someone talks: phone face down, no answer being planned while the other person is still speaking. A conversation like that can feel like being let into a room you forgot you had. Listening like that changes people. Guru Nanak's eighth pauri makes a much bigger claim: listening reaches all the way to earth and sky.
screen: `THE ONE WHO ACTUALLY STOPS.` → `THE PHONE, FACE DOWN.` → `LISTENING REACHES EARTH AND SKY.`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. By listening, people become siddhas, pirs, gods and masters of yoga. By listening, the earth, the bull that is said to hold it up, and the sky. By listening, the continents, the worlds and the regions below. By listening, death cannot touch you. Nanak, the devotees are always in bloom. By listening, pain and wrongdoing are wiped away. Listening to what? Sikh commentators answer: to the Name, to the shabad, the Guru's word. Suniai isn't just hearing noise; it's taking in the true Name until it rearranges you. Notice how the pauri moves. It starts with holy people, then gets huge: earth, sky, the old picture of the bull beneath the world, whole continents and underworlds. As if listening were no small, private hobby, but how things come to understand their place in everything. Later in Japji, Guru Nanak will gently reinterpret that bull, but that's for another day. Then the pauri comes close again, to one person: poh na sakai kaal, death can't touch you. Kaal is death, and time; the fear of it loses its grip. And the refrain: Naanak bhagtaa sadaa vigaas. Vigaas is the same flower word you met in pauri three, vigsai, blossoming: the devotees are always opening, like flowers. Suniai dookh paap kaa naas: by listening, pain and wrongdoing are destroyed. A big promise for something so quiet, and the same two lines will close each of the next three pauris.
screen: `SAGES AND MASTERS, BY LISTENING.` · `EARTH, BULL AND SKY.` · `DEATH CANNOT TOUCH.` · `VIGAAS — ALWAYS IN BLOOM.` · then, large: `BY LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Picture one person you'll talk to today: you're turned toward them, phone face down, listening fully without planning your reply, ready to ask one more question before you say anything about yourself. Then let the picture go and practice on the world, just listening to whatever is here. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru.
Suniai. By listening: sages, earth and sky; by listening, death cannot touch, and devotees are always in bloom.
Your line: by listening. Nanak, the devotees are always in bloom. That's day one hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the eighth pauri each morning; its refrain, that by listening pain and wrongdoing are wiped away, is why listening to Gurbani, in kirtan or katha, is itself treated as practice.

myth: Sikh readers take it as listening to the Name, the Guru's word.
the pauri says death cannot touch the one who listens
the refrain says devotees are always in bloom

fork.setup: the pauri lists what comes by listening: sages, earth, sky, worlds. then it comes close to one person. what does it promise?
fork.reveal: suniai poh na sakai kaal: by listening, death cannot touch you.

original.note: Gurmukhi: by listening, death cannot touch (Japji, pauri 8).

trapdoor: what you thought: listening is polite.
what it means: listening to the Name is what makes sages, holds the world, and loosens death's grip.
what a scholar hears: kaal means both death and time; the bull beneath the earth, dhaul, is reinterpreted later in Japji as dharma.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, the Japji, pauri 8

notes: Pauri 8 paraphrased after Macauliffe; not quoted.
'By listening, the earth, the bull and the sky' is kept literal; some translators read it as 'by listening, one understands the earth...'. Confirm preferred reading.
Teaser that pauri 16 reinterprets the bull as dharma: outline day 188. Confirm.
Outline practice 'listen fully to one person' adapted as an intention set during the sit plus a carry for later.
